source.note: Domain and task titles are preserved from the embedded app-data package. Study targets are app-authored paraphrased learning targets, not verbatim BRPT blueprint wording.

tasks.title: Patient information and clinical assessment
tasks.focus: Know the patient's reason for testing, symptoms, risk factors, medications, and baseline clinical picture before the study begins.
studyTargets: Review why the patient is being tested, what disorder is suspected, and which order or clinical question controls the pathway.
Recognize adult and pediatric clues for OSA, CSA, hypersomnolence, circadian disorders, parasomnias, and movement disorders.
Distinguish RLS from PLMS and PLMD: PLMS is a PSG finding; PLMD requires clinical impact and exclusion of better explanations.
Review iron status and medication history in RLS, and recognize earlier, stronger, or spreading symptoms as possible augmentation that needs clinician reassessment.
For hospitalized adults, treat OSA risk screening as entry to a diagnosis and management pathway, not as a definitive diagnosis.
tasks.nextAction: Review intake and disorder clues, then practice RLS/PLMD differentiation, inpatient screening boundaries, medications, and age-specific assessment.

tasks.title: Patient and caregiver education
tasks.focus: Explain the study clearly, reduce anxiety, set expectations, and give patient-centered instructions before lights out and before discharge.
studyTargets: Explain hookup, sensors, room setup, and why signal quality matters in plain language.
Teach pre-study, post-study, and discharge expectations without promising a diagnosis or treatment outcome.
Explain that inpatient OSA screening is part of a larger pathway and that follow-up testing may occur after stabilization or discharge.
Clarify the limitations of unattended, limited-channel, wearable, and app-generated sleep information.
Use age-appropriate, calm education that supports safety, comfort, and adherence.
tasks.nextAction: Study patient-facing explanations first, then practice calm education and caregiver-support scenarios.

tasks.title: Provide therapy support
tasks.focus: Support tolerance, comfort, and early success with PAP, oxygen, or other prescribed therapy-related needs.
studyTargets: Recognize barriers such as claustrophobia, poor fit, leaks, dryness, fear, and confusion.
Support established inpatient PAP or non-PAP therapy when feasible and not contraindicated, under current orders and hospital policy.
Monitor tolerance and adherence concerns, document barriers, and communicate them to the clinical team.
Recognize persistent central events as a reason for documentation and clinician reassessment rather than an automatic setting change.
Keep education, consultation, and discharge follow-up support within technologist scope and appropriate oversight.
tasks.nextAction: Focus on PAP comfort, desensitization, adherence support, download basics, and when to redirect to the clinical team.

tasks.title: Determine technical preparation
tasks.focus: Choose the correct setup, sensors, calibrations, and monitoring approach for the ordered study and the patient's clinical needs.
studyTargets: Match Type 1, Type 2, Type 3, or Type 4 capability to the ordered clinical question and patient suitability.
Use the correct PSG, PAP, split-night, MSLT, MWT, HSAT, pediatric, and clinically indicated additional channels.
Plan for CO2 monitoring, oxygen, seizure precautions, mobility, or other safety needs when ordered and appropriate.
Verify equipment, measurement function, controlled procedures, backup supplies, and required safety resources before testing.
Recognize that one- or two-signal studies and consumer devices cannot serve as universal substitutes for validated diagnostic testing.
tasks.nextAction: Review setup, sensors, electrode placement, filters, sampling, impedance, and standard precautions.

tasks.title: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
tasks.focus: Run the ordered study correctly from hookup through lights on while staying within guideline-based technologist practice.
studyTargets: Perform calibrations, biocals, signal checks, and troubleshooting methodically.
Follow the authorized workflow for attended PSG, limited-channel testing, PAP studies, MSLT, MWT, or HSAT support.
Preserve required signals and direct observation appropriate to the ordered study type.
Follow current controlled procedures, orders, device instructions, and safety requirements rather than inventing local rules.
Document key events, interventions, deviations, and technical issues as they happen.
tasks.nextAction: Practice the study workflow: PSG, pediatric PSG, MSLT/MWT, HSAT, safety, and documentation steps.

tasks.title: Identify, respond, and document
tasks.focus: Recognize clinically important changes during the study and respond safely while documenting what happened and what you did.
studyTargets: Identify artifact, lead loss, respiratory or rhythm concerns, behavioral events, and safety issues.
Respond using protocol: verify signals, assess the patient, and escalate when required.
Document recording type, usable signals, behavioral observations, technical adequacy, and limitations that affect interpretation.
Record nonconformities, corrective action, equipment failures, maintenance, and return-to-service checks according to facility workflow.
Protect data integrity, security, traceability, and retention while keeping the final record internally consistent.
tasks.nextAction: Study artifact, signal loss, equipment problems, abnormal events, calibrations, and what must be documented.

tasks.title: Score adult studies
tasks.focus: Apply adult scoring rules accurately and consistently across sleep stages, arousals, respiratory events, movements, and cardiac findings.
studyTargets: Score with the correct adult staging and event rules.
Separate obstructive, central, mixed, hypoventilation, and hypoxemia concepts correctly.
Watch thresholds carefully and avoid overcalling artifact as scored data.
Use source standards when the distinction is subtle or version-sensitive.
Think accuracy first: staging, then events, then totals and indexes.
tasks.nextAction: Study adult staging, arousals, respiratory events, desaturations, movements, and cardiac annotations.

tasks.title: Score pediatric and infant studies
tasks.focus: Use pediatric and infant scoring logic carefully, especially when thresholds and normal patterns differ from adults.
studyTargets: Know that normal breathing, arousals, and CO2 expectations differ in children and infants.
Use pediatric rules for events, hypoventilation, and stage-specific interpretation where required.
Be careful with age-based norms and developmental issues.
Do not force adult assumptions onto pediatric studies.
Document anything age-specific that affects interpretation.
tasks.nextAction: Review pediatric/infant scoring differences, especially respiratory duration rules, CO2/hypoventilation, and age-related patterns.

tasks.title: Generate and verify report
tasks.focus: Turn scored findings into a clean, internally consistent report with correct summaries, indexes, and supporting graphics.
studyTargets: Check totals, indexes, time-based calculations, graphs, tables, and narrative statements for internal consistency.
Use the correct terms for AHI, RDI, REI, sleep efficiency, latency, arousal data, and desaturation summaries.
Identify the recording type, usable signals, technical adequacy, behavioral observations, and important study limitations.
State whether the recording answered the ordered clinical question, especially for unattended and limited-channel studies.
Do not incorporate unvalidated consumer sleep stages or event estimates as PSG-equivalent findings.
tasks.nextAction: Practice calculations, report verification, indices, technologist notes, graphic summaries, and interpretation traps.

tasks.title: Administer PAP therapy
tasks.focus: Recognize when PAP is being applied correctly, when it needs adjustment, and when the patient is not tolerating it well.
studyTargets: Know the purpose and boundaries of CPAP, APAP, BPAP, BPAP with a backup rate, ASV, and ventilation-support pathways.
For CSA, distinguish backup-rate BPAP from BPAP without backup and avoid applying obstructive-pressure logic to persistent central events.
Treat ASV eligibility as a current clinician and device-specific safety review, not as one historical ejection-fraction rule.
Support continuation of established inpatient PAP when feasible, documenting device, mode, interface, settings, tolerance, and safety concerns.
Use protocol-based recognition, documentation, and escalation; do not independently prescribe modes or change settings.
tasks.nextAction: Study PAP modality separation, leak/interface troubleshooting, persistent central-event reassessment, ASV safety routing, and inpatient therapy continuity.

tasks.title: Identify alternative therapies
tasks.focus: Recognize non-PAP therapy pathways and when the record or patient history points toward them.
studyTargets: Know common non-PAP pathways such as oral appliance therapy, positional therapy, surgery, weight management, and selected stimulation therapies.
Recognize acetazolamide and transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation as clinician-directed adult CSA alternatives without teaching dosing or procedure steps.
For adult RLS, recognize iron therapy and alpha-2-delta ligands as current priorities and augmentation risk with routine dopamine-agonist use.
Support continuation of established inpatient oral-appliance or hypoglossal-nerve-stimulation therapy when feasible and not contraindicated.
Keep candidate selection, medication choice, dosing, and treatment changes at recognition and escalation level.
tasks.nextAction: Review oral appliances, surgery/stimulation, current RLS treatment awareness, adult CSA alternatives, and inpatient non-PAP continuity.

tasks.title: Administer oxygen therapy
tasks.focus: Recognize oxygen-related orders, monitoring needs, and response patterns while following safety and protocol rules.
studyTargets: Separate oxygenation support from treatment of upper-airway obstruction or inadequate ventilation.
Recognize current low-flow oxygen indication awareness for selected heart-failure and high-altitude CSA pathways.
Do not infer oxygen flow, titration steps, or a universal inpatient oxygen protocol from treatment guidelines.
Document ordered flow, timing, response, device/interface context, and safety concerns according to protocol.
Watch CO2 and hypoventilation risk when relevant and escalate rather than treating saturation alone.
tasks.nextAction: Study oxygenation versus ventilation, selected CSA indication awareness, ordered titration workflow, documentation, and CO2 safety.
